title: Wish it as it comes
hook: don't demand that things happen as you wish, but wish them as they happen (Enchiridion 8)

segments.voice: Yesterday: when the captain calls. Your line was listen for the call. Did you put one pleasure down the first time you were called? Day three hundred forty.

You planned a picnic. It rains. You can spend the afternoon at the window, arguing with the sky, replaying the forecast that said ten percent. Or you can spread the blanket on the living room floor and eat the sandwiches there, listening to the rain on the roof. Same rain, either way. The difference is which direction your wishing points. Toward the day you wanted, or toward the day that came. Section eight of the handbook flips the usual arrow of wishing around. Today: wish it as it comes.
screen: `THE PICNIC, THE RAIN.` → `ARGUING WITH THE SKY.` → `WHICH WAY DOES THE WISH POINT?`

segments.voice: First, the line. In George Long's translation: "Seek not that the things which happen should happen as you wish; but wish the things which happen to be as they are, and you will have a tranquil flow of life." Second, the flip. The usual order is to wish first and then wait to see if the world agrees. Epictetus says let the world go first. Then wish for what came. It sounds like a trick, and in a way it is: a way of making sure your wishes and the world never fight. The prize he names is a smooth flow: the Greek verb pictures a stream running without snags. Third, an older Stoic image. A later Christian writer, Hippolytus, reports that the early Stoics Zeno and Chrysippus compared us to a dog tied to a cart. If the dog wants to follow, it walks along, both pulled and willing. If it doesn't, it's dragged anyway. Either way the cart goes. The only choice is whether to trot or be dragged. Fourth, what it doesn't mean. This isn't Epictetus telling anyone to welcome cruelty or stop working for change. The handbook already sorted things into two piles. Your choices, your effort, your voice: those are yours, and you use them fully. What it asks is that once something has actually happened, the rain, the canceled flight, the result, you stop demanding it be otherwise. Centuries later the philosopher Nietzsche put a cousin of this idea into two Latin words: amor fati, love of fate. Epictetus' version is plainer. Not love, necessarily. Just: as it comes.
screen: `SEEK NOT THAT THINGS HAPPEN AS YOU WISH.` · `LET THE WORLD GO FIRST.` · `THE DOG AND THE CART.` · `WHAT IT DOESN'T MEAN.` · then, large: `AS IT COMES.`

segments.voice: Sit and listen for a moment to whatever is happening around you right now. A car, a fan, a voice in the next room, maybe silence. Don't wish any of it different. Let each sound arrive, and quietly wish it to be exactly as it is. Then bring to mind one small surprise from today that you didn't plan. A delay, a message, a change of weather. Turn toward it the same way, and say inside: as it comes. The bell holds the time.
Wish it as it comes. Epictetus' flip: don't ask things to happen as you wish; wish them as they happen, and life flows. Today's word.
screen: `WISH IT AS IT COMES — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: as it comes. When today surprises you, even a little, say the line before you say anything else, and see what's possible from there. Day three hundred forty.

howItsDone: People who practice Stoicism often try to accept what has already happened as it is, while still putting full effort into what is up to them next.

fork.setup: you're the dog tied to the cart, and the cart starts moving. what do you do?
options: dig in your paws and refuse.
fork.reveal: in the Stoic image the cart goes either way; the dog can follow willingly, or be dragged.

original.note: Greek: a good flow, life running smoothly; Enchiridion 8 uses the verb form.

trapdoor: what you thought: just accept whatever happens.
what it means: once a thing has happened, wish it as it is, and keep acting fully in what is yours.
what a scholar hears: euroia biou, the smooth flow of life, was Zeno's own definition of happiness, according to later reports.

sources.quoted: Seek not that the things which happen should happen as you wish; but wish the things which happen to be as they are, and you will have a tranquil flow of life.

notes: Review (2026-10-01): cut the count 'two lines long'; the text uses a verb, not the noun euroia, so the teach and the original-word note now say so; softened 'usually we wish first'.
εὔροια in Enchiridion 8 (the verb εὐροήσεις); 'euroia biou' as Zeno's definition of happiness (Stobaeus, Ecl. 2.77): confirm.
Dog-and-cart image: Hippolytus, Refutation 1.21, attributing it to Zeno and Chrysippus; confirm reference.
Nietzsche's amor fati: The Gay Science 276 (1882); confirm section number.
